TRANSCRIPT OF PROCEEDINGS
THE HON CATHERINE HOLMES AC SC, Commissioner
THE ROYAL COMMISSION INTO THE ROBODEBT SCHEME
WEDNESDAY, 25 JANUARY 2023 AT 9.36 AM (AEST)
DAY 25
MR JUSTIN GREGGERY KC, Senior Counsel Assisting
MR ANGUS SCOTT KC, Senior Counsel Assisting
MS SALWA MARSH, Counsel Assisting
MS DOMINIQUE HOGAN-DORAN SC, for the Commonwealth
MR ALEX VIAL, for the Commonwealth

COMMISSIONER: I just have a couple of things before we get started. As will be evident, we
are still having sound problems. I'm told there is some replacement equipment coming at
lunch time, but if the sound should drop out what we must all do is just sit silently until it
comes back on, which apparently will not be long. So we won't be adjourning if there's a
sound drop-out. We will just sit and wait. You can sing if you like, Mr Scott. That couldn't do
any harm. But nothing will be recorded. So we've got to bear that in mind.
Number 2, what I propose to do for the rest of this Hearing Block, at any rate, is to
endeavour to extend the sitting hours by taking an hour for lunch and sitting until 5 o'clock
as a general rule. Which I appreciate will put an enormous burden on people because the
time out of the hearing is usually spent in preparation, the need for which is extensive. But in
order to get through the witness list, I think we are just going to have to manage it. So that's
the plan, Ms Hogan-Doran. I think you've been warned.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Thank you, Commissioner, I will be here.
COMMISSIONER: Good. Thank you. Alright. Now, you're appearing, Mr Scott?
MR SCOTT: I am, Commissioner, if it pleases. I appear with Ms Marsh for the first
witnesses - the first two witnesses today, Ms Bundy and Mr Brazel.
COMMISSIONER: And the appearance for the Commonwealth is the same or not?
MS HOGAN-DORAN: No, Commissioner. I appear today with my learned friend Mr Vial.
COMMISSIONER: Mr Vial. Thank you. Alright. Yes, Ms Bundy we have got you back. Thank
you.
<ELIZABETH ANNE BUNDY, ON FORMER AFFIRMATION
<EXAMINATION BY MR SCOTT KC
MR SCOTT: Ms Bundy, you will recall yesterday in our discussion you conveyed your
understanding of the legal position in 2017 when you were head of the Appeals Branch as
being that it was permissible for decision-makers under the Robodebt Scheme to rely on the
best information they had available to them, that is, the information, in effect, in the
possession of the Department without making any further inquiries.
MS BUNDY: Yes, unless that was displaced by other information.
MR SCOTT: Sure. But in circumstances where, to take the EIC and CUPI Schemes as examples,
two genuine attempts had been made to contact the recipient and those attempts had
failed, your understanding was that it was perfectly lawful for the Compliance Officer to rely
on the information which they had available to them without making inquiries with
employers.

MS BUNDY: Yes, and that was based on the legal advice.
MR SCOTT: Yes. And that's what I wanted to confirm. That -
MS BUNDY: Yes, that was the position that I understood, absolutely.
MR SCOTT: And you understood that because you had been advised by lawyers to that
effect?
MS BUNDY: I'm just trying to remember the sequence of my understanding. I - when I first
started, I think I made inquiries with Mark Withnell, who advised this is a long-standing
practice of the agency. I said - and I don't know who to - and I had - well, somehow I had an
understanding that DSS will -
MR SCOTT: Can I briefly interrupt you, Ms Bundy.
MS BUNDY: Yes.
MR SCOTT: I don't want to cut you off, but you said you were advised by Mark Withnell that
this was a long-standing practice of the agency.
MS BUNDY: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Does that refer to a statement that it was a long-standing practice of the agency
to rely on averaging without making any inquiries of employers?
MS BUNDY: No, it was that, in the past, you - the process was that - to inquire with
employers, and sometimes they couldn't be found and sometimes they didn't respond to
information, and it was in those circumstances where the ATO information would be used.
MR SCOTT: Okay. Alright. So I interrupted you, Ms Bundy. So I think you were purporting -
MS BUNDY: Yes, and the change in my mind was that we weren't going to employers
anymore, and I don't know who I spoke to, but somehow I got a view or an understanding
that DSS had said from the policy agency perspective yes, and then I was fairly comfortable
that that was okay.
MR SCOTT: So you haven't mentioned any lawyers in that sequence. I just want to clarify, did
you get legal advice or were you informed of legal advice by a lawyer that it was okay?
MS BUNDY: I'm just trying to recall. I had - I know from looking at my records that Maris sent
me some advice on 2 March 2017, and I think that was the DSS advice, and I also had a view
for some time - I'm not sure informed by what - that there had been external legal advice
from DSS, and I can't find a record of receiving internal legal advice - like, written advice, but
I did have a conversation in the context of the appeals about ‘does this mean that we now
need to get payslips’.

MR SCOTT: By Maris, are you referring to Maris Stipnieks?
MS BUNDY: Yes.
MR SCOTT: He provided you - forwarded something to you on 2 March 2017?
MS BUNDY: He copied me into something, yes.
MR SCOTT: Have you produced or caused that document to be produce to the Commission?
MS BUNDY: I referred to it in my Statement.
MR SCOTT: Whereabouts?
MS BUNDY: Paragraph 146.
MR SCOTT: Paragraph 146; is that right?
MS BUNDY: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Alright. And that has a footnote 122, and that footnote refers to four documents.
Is that right?
MS BUNDY: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And is that a document which contains - is one of those documents the email
from Mr Stipnieks on 2 March 2017?
MS BUNDY: Yes, that would be correct. So I think what had happened, Maris had cc'd me
into the email to someone else. At that point in time, I must have recalled receiving
something from Maris and my office has found that, and at that time, given Professor
Carney's article, I think there was - from Jason McNamara or the Deputy Secretary, to
forward that on to them.
MR SCOTT: So Professor Carney's article?
MS BUNDY: Yes.
MR SCOTT: What Professor Carney article are you referring to?
MS BUNDY: The one from April 2018.
MR SCOTT: Right, but that's obviously after 2 March 2017.
MS BUNDY: Yes.

MR SCOTT: Okay. So I'm just focusing at the moment on 2 March 2017 and what you were
forwarded from Mr Stipnieks.
MS BUNDY: I don't - I don't recall now receiving it, and I looked at the email and I asked my
office to print it.
MR SCOTT: So when did you ask your office to print it?
MS BUNDY: I think I - I don't know what day it was. I can check. But the email trail, I said
please print.
MR SCOTT: This is in 2018 after coming to -
MS BUNDY: 2017.
MR SCOTT: Okay. I see. Right. And is your recollection that - we are just trying to bring it up,
Ms Bundy, we don't have it to hand. Is your recollection that that contained advice regarding
the issue of averaging?
MS BUNDY: I - my recollection is that it contains the email that DSS sent to the Ombudsman's
Office, with some attached advices.
MR SCOTT: I see. Right. Okay. Can we, please, have brought up on the screen Exhibit 2,
DSS.5006.0003.1833. Can we have brought up on the screen Exhibit 3? Actually, instead can
we bring up on the screen Doc ID CTH.2000.0007.5664. Do you recognise that document,
Ms Bundy?
MS BUNDY: I don't.
MR SCOTT: Is that not the document that you are referring to as having been forwarded to
you by Mr Stipnieks?
MS BUNDY: I - it well could be the document, but I have to say, I haven't - there's been so
many sort of bits and pieces going on, I have to actually just go and check that that was
actually the document attached to the document. Yes, from memory, there was advice from
2014 and 2017, and there's a covering email from DSS to the Ombudsman.
MR SCOTT: Okay. Can I just get you to look at paragraph 146 of your Statement, which you
should have in front of you?
MS BUNDY: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And you will recall footnote 122, which is at the end of that paragraph.
MS BUNDY: Yes.

MS BUNDY: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And if you look at that footnote, have a look at the Doc ID for the last document
footnoted in footnote 122?
MS BUNDY: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Yes. Satisfied that that's what we are talking about in?
MS BUNDY: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Thank you. Alright. Commissioner, this document hasn't been tendered yet.
Perhaps it could be tendered.
COMMISSIONER: Okay. So what are we going to - I haven't got an exhibit list in front of me,
I'm afraid.
MR SCOTT: I'm just getting a number for you, Commissioner. Could it be numbered 3588A?
COMMISSIONER: Right. It will be 3588A.
<EXHIBIT 3588A TENDERED AND MARKED
MR SCOTT: Thank you, Commissioner. Can we just call out the section under the heading
2017 Advice. Thank you. And, Ms Bundy, can you read that section to yourself and then I will
ask you some questions about it.
MS BUNDY: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Have you read that? Do you understand that to be advice provided by DSS in
2017?
MS BUNDY: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Do you understand that to say, in the first sentence in that section, that is:
...to identify the question for which advice was being provided, being about whether using
income averaging as a last resort to determine a social security debt was lawful in
circumstances where no other information about the person's circumstances are available.
Do you see that?
MS BUNDY: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Do you see the words "last resort"?

MS BUNDY: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And I think your evidence is that is not how Robodebt operated. Is it? That is, it
was not using averaging as a last resort.
MS BUNDY: No, it was not.
MR SCOTT: So the advice - sorry, the question that is being answered in this advice is
irrelevant to the lawfulness of the Robodebt Scheme, isn't it?
MS BUNDY: No.
MR SCOTT: Why is that?
MS BUNDY: Because while the question is talking about a last resort, I think people's
understanding of what "last resort" mean - can mean can differ, and I think from the
agency's perspective that this was similar to language used previously where averaging was
done on a last-resort basis where we went to get employer information. Whereas the
advice - and I'm just reading down there - that - which effectively was read and taken to
be - and I'm saying this in hindsight, because I'm not sure I actually read this advice in 2017
because it was copied to me and it was very busy time and I think I read the first email that
was attached, as opposed to really digging into the advice. But I read this, and it talks about
as long as the person has been given the opportunity to provide the information, then that
information can be used.
MR SCOTT: In - as a last resort.
MS BUNDY: As long as they were given - that's right, as long as they were given the
opportunity to provide further information, that information can then be used.
MR SCOTT: In circumstances where there had been two failed attempts to contact the social
security recipient under CUPI and EIC, averaging was applied; correct?
MS BUNDY: Yes. On the basis that that was the best available information to the
decision-maker and there was no duty to inquire under administrative law to obtain further
information.
MR SCOTT: And there was no attempts whatsoever made to seek information from other
sources, even if those other sources might provide readily available information.
MS BUNDY: Yes, at - if the person had not engaged. That's correct.
MR SCOTT: It's plainly not using averaging as a last resort, is it, Ms Bundy?
MS BUNDY: I would say that's correct in those circumstances, yes. That is not - I also
probably wouldn't say what we were doing previously as being a last resort activity either.

MR SCOTT: Can we just bring that section that's highlighted there down.
COMMISSIONER: What do you mean by that?
MR SCOTT: Sorry, I just didn't want that section highlighted so I can take -
COMMISSIONER: Did you look at that advice in any detail?
MS BUNDY: In 2017, I don't think I did. I think what I did was read the overarching email that
was sent to the Ombudsman, that said this is consistent with legislation.
COMMISSIONER: Because if you look at it now, you can see that there's no reference to any
case law. And no reference to any section which authorises any legislative provision which
authorises averaging. And it doesn't seem much more than, "I think it will be a fair thing",
really?
MS BUNDY: It was supplemented - and I don't think I have got a copy of it - I couldn't find a
copy of it - as I understood by other internal DHS advice. And for some reason I had a view
that there had been external advice at the time of the NPP, but I'm not sure how I had that
view.
MR SCOTT: Can we just go to the next page of the document, please? No, the previous page,
I beg your pardon. Were you aware that, in 2014, the Department of Social Services had
given earlier advice about the use of averaging?
MS BUNDY: My recollection is that I had read that in the covering email that had been sent
to the Ombudsman by DSS.
MR SCOTT: Right. And you were aware that that advice said that averaging is unlawful?
MS BUNDY: Yes, I - my view for a very long time was that DSS had provided advice in 2014,
that that was on the basis that we would just be getting the information and averaging and
not asking people to - you know, affording them procedural fairness, and that once DSS
understood that that wasn't the process, then that was okay. There was a - as I understood
it, that there was a change in the proposal at that point in time. And that - and perhaps that's
why I thought there had been external advice. I'm not sure.
MR SCOTT: Can I just get you to have a look at what's on the screen there. Doc ID
CTH.2000.0007.5666. Do you see the heading 2014 Advice?
MS BUNDY: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Do you see what it says there:
You have asked whether a debt amount derived from annual smoothing or smoothing over a
defined period of time is legally defensible.

MS BUNDY: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And the answer is:
In our view, a debt amount derived from annual smoothing or smoothing over a defined
period of time may not be derived consistently with the legislative framework.
MS BUNDY: Yes.
MR SCOTT: It's clear advice, isn't it, that smoothing, which is another way of referring to
averaging, is unlawful.
MS BUNDY: Yes, that it wasn't consistent with the legislative framework, yes.
MR SCOTT: Right. And so - and you read this advice as well as the 2017 advice for which
we've just -
MS BUNDY: I don't think I did read the advices. I think I read the covering email.
MR SCOTT: I see. But the earlier advice, the 2017 advice that refers to last resort, you caused
to be printed out on 2 - on or about 2 March 2017.
MS BUNDY: Yes, I had asked my office to just print documents, put them in the pile of things
to get to.
MR SCOTT: And didn't read it?
MS BUNDY: My recollection is that I read the covering email that had been provided to the
Ombudsman's Office.
MR SCOTT: Wasn't the lawfulness of the use of averaging as it applied in the Robodebt
Scheme of central importance to your role insofar as you were the manager of the branch
that had the AROs within it making decisions under the Robodebt Scheme?
MS BUNDY: I think the lawfulness of the Scheme was central to all decision-makers.
MR SCOTT: So wasn't it central and important to your role to actually read the legal advices
on the question of averaging?
MS BUNDY: Yes, I think people probably should read all legal advices.
MR SCOTT: Why didn't you?
MS BUNDY: It was an extremely busy time. I had come into the role on 10 February. There
had been a lot of work already done. I had perhaps made the assumption that these things
had effectively been resolved. I read the email that went to the Ombudsman that said DSS

MR SCOTT: Excuse me. Commissioner, I need to take the witness to a document which is
referred to in the witness' Statement but hasn't been - it's an email that hasn't got
redactions on it. It might be necessary for it to be shown in hard copy to the witness so that -
COMMISSIONER: Okay. Have you got a copy for me?
MR SCOTT: I've only got one copy.
COMMISSIONER: Okay.
MR SCOTT: If we can put it up on the screen but not put it on the live stream, we can do that.
The document is CTH.2000.0007.5662. Do you see that, Ms Bundy?
MS BUNDY: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And just for your reference, if you go to your paragraph 146, footnote 22, you
can see that it's got the Document ID for the second-last document referred to in that
footnote?
MS BUNDY: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And would you agree with me that is the covering email that would have
been - that that earlier document I showed you would have had attached to it?
MS BUNDY: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Okay. And is this what you understood to be the advice provided to the
Ombudsman?
MS BUNDY: Yes.
COMMISSIONER: Aren't you calling Mr de Burgh today?
MR SCOTT: Yes.
COMMISSIONER: Won't that exist in a redacted form somewhere?
MR SCOTT: It might be in a different Document ID. And I don't have Mr de Burgh. Sorry,
Commissioner.
COMMISSIONER: Okay.
MR SCOTT: Now -
COMMISSIONER: So what are we getting from this?

MR SCOTT: I'm just trying to find it, Commissioner. I haven't marked this up. So, firstly, does
this record what you understood to be the subsequent advice that explained the change of
position that you were referring to earlier, Ms Bundy?
MS BUNDY: Yes, I understood that the proposal previously wasn't going to allow people to
respond to information, and then I think it's - the key difference, the average income is only
used for the purpose of (indistinct) when no other information is available, and attempts
have been made to seek information from the individual.
MR SCOTT: What part of - are you referring to where it says "no other information is
available"?
MS BUNDY: So:
A key difference between the measure as DSS originally understood it and the approach that
was ultimately implemented is that average income is only used for the purpose of
calculating a (indistinct) when no other information is available and attempts have been
made to seek information from it the individual.
MR SCOTT: Yes. And that could only be reconciled with the 2017 advice to which we've just
identified. "If no other information is available" is a reference to the words "last resort."
Don't you agree?
MS BUNDY: Yes - I think that's right. In hindsight, you could read it in that way. The way that
was read was that the information available to the decision-maker in front of them.
MR SCOTT: Do you agree that - so you now accept that the statement "no other information
is available" is inaccurate in that part of the email?
MS BUNDY: I think people's understanding of what that meant could be different.
MR SCOTT: Including the words in that advice, that 2017 advice to which we've just referred
to where the words were explicitly "last resort".
MS BUNDY: As I said, I think people's understanding of what certain things mean can differ.
MR SCOTT: Including the words "last resort".
MS BUNDY: Yes, I think the words "last resort" can differ. People's understanding of what
that means, yes.
MR SCOTT: In circumstances where the previous advice, the 2014 advice, had been that
averaging is unlawful.
MS BUNDY: So, as I've said, in the past, we used to attempt to get payslips from employers,
and we called that - if we couldn't do that, we called that last resort. Could we have actually

done more and sought further information, asked for bank statements at that point? Yes. So
is last resort in that context a last resort?
MR SCOTT: So just so I'm clear, what you are saying is that the view as to what constituted
last resort changed in the implementation of the Robodebt Scheme?
MS BUNDY: No, what I'm saying is that I think people's understanding of what last resort can
mean can differ. And as is what is the best available information.
MR SCOTT: Surely last resort means there's no other options available?
MS BUNDY: Yes, and in the past where we had gone to employers and that was the step
taken and we would average the information, we called that last resort. That did not
necessarily mean that there was no other options available.
COMMISSIONER: When this thing started, DHS officers weren't even looking at the DHS file
to see if there was anything on there that explained anything. And people were accepting
that as a last resort, were they? The information, the employment separation certificate
which might clear things up is on the file, but we regard ourselves - because the information
is here from the Tax Office - as in a last resort position?
MS BUNDY: No, Commissioner, I think that was an incorrect position and that was, from
memory, referred to in the Ombudsman's report, that if you - you must consider all the
information you have available to you in the records of what's in front of the decision-maker.
And so that was corrected.
MR SCOTT: What about a situation where it's obvious from the file that there is a reasonable
prospect that, with a simple inquiry with the employer, the assumptions underpinning an
averaging calculation would be falsified?
MS BUNDY: So, there was - and my recollection is after - in 2017, where there was, for
example, you know, averaging would result in an amount that was not a - you know, a pay
rate or a very anomalous type of pay rate, that - then averaging wasn't applied in those
circumstances.
MR SCOTT: Can I show you an example of what I'm referring to. Perhaps, Commissioner, this
document should also be made an exhibit and the previous document the witness was taken
to. Yes. Perhaps 3588B and 3588C.
COMMISSIONER: Alright. What is it, before I make it an exhibit?
MR SCOTT: Thank you, Commissioner. Ms Bundy, you have your AAT decisions bundle in
front of you that you were provided overnight?
MS BUNDY: Yes.

MR SCOTT: If you go to tab 3 of that bundle. That should be Exhibit 3461, Doc ID
CTH.0032.0002.0020.
MS BUNDY: Yes.
MR SCOTT: If that could be brought up on the screen. Have you had an opportunity to review
this decision overnight?
MS BUNDY: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Thank you. And, for completeness, do you accept that this is the first case listed
in the AAT OCI case summaries document, which should be behind your tab 2, which is
document Exhibit 3460, Doc ID 3007.0006.1949?
MS BUNDY: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Same case?
MS BUNDY: Mmm.
MR SCOTT: And the case summaries document is a document you had provided to you in
2017?
MS BUNDY: This is not the case summaries document provided to me in 2017.
MR SCOTT: Were you aware of the case that we are referring to in 2017?
MS BUNDY: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Okay. Thank you. If you go back to the case, please. If you go to the first - the
second page of the document. The first paragraph, call that out, please. This social security
recipient gave birth to a child on 17 June 2014.
MS BUNDY: Yes.
MR SCOTT: As a consequence, she claimed parenting payment for which she was paid from
17 July 2014 until 16 June 2015.
MS BUNDY: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And that's - the fact that she was giving birth to a child would be why she would
be claiming that payment; correct?
MS BUNDY: You would assume so, yes.
MR SCOTT: But notwithstanding that, there was a decision made on 11 October 2016 that

MS BUNDY: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Part of the Online Compliance Intervention process?
MS BUNDY: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And if we go to paragraph 2 and call that out, the recipient sought review of this
decision and an ARO reviewed the available evidence was - but was unable to speak with the
recipient.
MS BUNDY: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And there was a decision made to treat - to average her income using the ATO
data?
MS BUNDY: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And so that even though she wasn't working over those two weeks while she had
a child, it was deemed that she had earned income over that period.
MS BUNDY: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And part of the calculation involved - if we go to paragraph 10 - I'm sorry,
paragraph 3.
COMMISSIONER: Well, she was actually on unpaid leave from October to March. It wasn't
just the two weeks you referred to that she wasn't working.
MR SCOTT: That's right. And so the process of this decision was to calculate - to average out
her income across the entire period, including, if we go to paragraph 10, was in receipt of
paid parental leave. Do you see that?
MS BUNDY: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And paid parental leave is a source of income that is not assessable for the
purpose of the income test; correct?
MS BUNDY: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And so the decision erroneously took into account as part of her income amounts
paid as paid parental leave, which shouldn't have been taken into account. Correct?
MS BUNDY: Yes.

MR SCOTT: And would you accept that the circumstances of this case demonstrate that it
would have been a very easy exercise to make inquiries with the employer to ascertain the
true state of her income and what she was doing on leave?
MS BUNDY: I would say in respect of this case that it was in 2016. The - the review and
decision and obviously the AAT decision was in 2017, and there had been changes made. So,
yes, could inquiries have been made with the employer previous to the applicant
engaging - obviously, once someone engaged there was a different process that came about.
But equally there were circumstances - and, as I said, where - and we continued
to - approach the continuous improvement where if there were circumstances that where
averaging wouldn't seem to be the right approach, it - and I'm not sure, from memory, what
the process then became, whether or not there were inquiries made with the employer or in
actual fact we just stopped the review.
MR SCOTT: Well, let's take it in steps. Do you accept that on no view could it be said - on no
view at all could it be said that, in these circumstances, averaging had been applied as a last
resort.
MS BUNDY: No.
MR SCOTT: Do you accept that or not?
MS BUNDY: Yes, I accept that we were not using averaging as a last resort.
MR SCOTT: Right. Okay. And the only advice that you have been able to identify as
supporting the use of averaging in March of 2017 was an advice that said you could do it as a
last resort.
MS BUNDY: Yes, that is what the advice said at that time. As I've said, I read the email from
DSS to the Ombudsman, is my recollection. I took from that that DSS had said this is
consistent with the legislative requirements and that we could make decisions based on the
best available information in front of the decision-maker.
MR SCOTT: Where there is no other information available.
MS BUNDY: In front of the decision-maker at that point in time and, under administrative
law, there was no duty to make further inquiries.
MR SCOTT: Alright.
COMMISSIONER: Where did that last bit come from?
MS BUNDY: That was advice provided from Annette Musolino and Maris Stipnieks.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you.

MR SCOTT: Thank you. Alright. That document can be taken down. You state in your
Statement at paragraph 19, I think, that one of - your role included reporting on the
performance of the review process and as appropriate, escalate issues to the Service
Delivery Roundtable. Do you recall saying that?
MS BUNDY: Yes.
MR SCOTT: What was the Service Delivery Roundtable?
MS BUNDY: The Service Delivery Roundtable was what we would call a tier 2 committee. So
you would have the Executive Committee and then a range of committees that reported
through to the Executive Committee, and the Service Delivery Roundtable was one of those
committees.
MR SCOTT: Right. When you say it was a tier 2 committee, what level of people were on it?
MS BUNDY: I don't recall specifically who was on it, and our membership changed, but it
would be Secretary and/or Deputy Secretary and Band 2s, would be my expectation, but the
Department or agency should be able to check that in its records.
MR SCOTT: So Secretary and Deputy Secretary as a minimum, ordinarily.
MS BUNDY: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And in reporting to the Service Delivery Roundtable, was it part of your role to
report on the outcome of AAT decisions?
MS BUNDY: No.
MR SCOTT: Okay. Well, can I just ask you - could the witness please be shown - in your
bundle, Ms Bundy, it's tab 16 of your main bundle, I believe. Exhibit 3544. Doc ID
CTH.2001.0006.1296. Alright. Now, Ms Bundy, can you see that's an email from yourself
dated 19 April 2017?
MS BUNDY: Yes.
MR SCOTT: It's addressed to, among others, Damien Brazel and Annette Musolino?
MS BUNDY: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And you state - and it's also addressed to someone called Alison McCann. Who
was Alison McCann?
MS BUNDY: She was the acting general manager of the Compliance division.
MR SCOTT: Okay. You see in that email you say - do you accept in you say in that email:

Hi Damien, Annette and Alison,
See this week's SDRT report.
MS BUNDY: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Do you agree that week's Service Delivery Roundtable report?
MS BUNDY: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And you were you say:
We are going to pull together the list of the 10 set aside decisions relating to the OCI. We
need to have a better feedback loop with these, I think, where we aren't appealing and how
we are going to manage and then ensure feedback goes back down regarding decisions.
Do you see that?
